The epidemiology of [[atrieflimren|atrial fibrillation]] (AF) in [[Danmark|Denmark]] represents a significant and growing public health focus, systematically tracked by the [[Databasen for Atrieflimren i Danmark|Danish Atrial Fibrillation Database]] and the [[Landspatientregisteret|National Patient Registry]]. Annually, more than 20,000 Danes are diagnosed with AF, and over 130,000 individuals live with the condition [^src3] [^src10] [^src22]. Recent annual reports detail a steady increase in both incident and prevalent cases: from 19,671 incident and 134,810 prevalent patients in the 2022–2023 period [^src7] [^src11], to 22,073 incident and 136,420 prevalent cases in 2023–2024 [^src14], and 22,250 incident and 138,889 prevalent cases in 2024–2025 [^src19]. The national incidence rate was recorded at 3.7 per 1,000 inhabitants in the recent reporting periods [^src23]. Demographically, the average age at diagnosis for incident patients is 74 years, while the overall average age of prevalent patients is 70 years [^src18] [^src23]. Regional prevalence also varies, with [[Region Sjælland|Region Zealand]] reporting a prevalence of 27.1 per 1,000 inhabitants in 2024/2025 [^src23].

AF carries substantial risks of severe cardiovascular and neurological complications. The lifetime risk of developing [[hjertesvigtsindikatoren|heart failure]] following an AF diagnosis is 40%, making it the most common cardiovascular cause of death globally among this patient group [^src13] [^src22]. Thromboembolic and bleeding events are closely monitored through national quality indicators. The national incidence of [[Iskæmisk apopleksi|ischemic stroke]] among prevalent AF patients remains stable at approximately 0.8% [^src8] [^src15] [^src20]. Concurrently, the risk of [[Intrakraniel blødning|intracranial bleeding]] is observed in about 0.5% of prevalent patients [^src4] [^src12] [^src16]. [[Alvorlig blødning|Severe bleeding]] events result in hospitalizations for roughly 2.2% of prevalent patients annually, with regional admission rates varying slightly between 1.9% and 2.3% [^src9] [^src17] [^src21]. For newly diagnosed (incident) patients, the one-year risk of severe bleeding is approximately 3.1% to 3.2% [^src9] [^src17]. Notably, a significant proportion of bleeding events (43.7%) occur in patients with a low [[CHA2DS2-VASc]] score of 0 or 1, highlighting the complexity of bleeding risk stratification [^src17]. Despite the increased use of [[antikoagulationsbehandling|anticoagulation therapy]], there has been no significant real-term reduction in the proportion of severe bleeding events over recent years [^src9] [^src21].

The management and healthcare delivery for AF patients also exhibit distinct epidemiological patterns. Persistence to anticoagulation therapy has shown an increasing trend since 2016, generally remaining at a high level compared to international standards [^src2] [^src5]. While the vast majority of AF patients are managed within the public hospital system, a small subset is treated by [[Praktiserende kardiologer|private practicing cardiologists]]. For instance, out of all incident cases, only 1,064 (4.8%) were seen in private cardiology practices, with stark regional disparities: 790 incident patients were treated in the [[Region Hovedstaden|Capital Region]], compared to zero in the [[Region Syddanmark|Region of Southern Denmark]] [^src6]. Furthermore, quality outcomes such as severe bleeding rates show minor variations not only across the five Danish [[regioner|regions]] but also at the local [[sundhedsklynger|health cluster]] level, where bleeding rates fluctuated between 1.9% and 2.7% [^src21]. These comprehensive epidemiological insights, compiled in the [[Årsrapport 2023|annual reports]] by the [[Regionernes Kliniske Kvalitetsudviklingsprogram|Danish Regions' Clinical Quality Development Program]], underscore the ongoing need for balanced stroke prevention and bleeding risk management in the Danish AF population.
